entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Samuel Hearne (unknown–1792) was a British explorer and naturalist who led the first recorded expedition to map the Mackenzie River in what is now Canada. During his journey, he encountered the Dene people and learned about their culture, collecting valuable information on the region's flora and fauna. Hearne's accounts of his travels and discoveries were published in several books, providing insight into the natural history of the Canadian wilderness. His expeditions played a significant role in shaping British understanding of the region and its Indigenous peoples.

Hearne's work was influenced by the scientific discoveries of the Enlightenment, which emphasized the importance of empirical observation and classification. He was also part of a broader network of explorers who mapped the Canadian wilderness during this period, including David Thompson and John Stuart.

The legacy of Samuel Hearne's expeditions can be seen in modern conservation efforts aimed at preserving Canada's natural heritage. His work also highlights the complex relationships between European colonizers and Indigenous peoples in North America.

As a naturalist, Hearne's contributions to the field of entomology are still recognized today, with several species named after him in recognition of his discoveries.
